claim: A viral video shows a police officer in Cumbria, England arresting a young boy for fishing, with the footage showing the boy being handcuffed as a result of fishing.
label: False
ruling: False. Cumbria Police said this clip shows officers responding last year to a report of a child in possession of a knife, and the interaction had no connection to fishing. No knife was found and no arrests were made.

claim: A Facebook post claims that income tax and the other taxes on its list did not exist 100 years ago, and that the UK had no national debt a century ago.
label: Mostly false
ruling: Partly false. Income tax was first introduced in 1799 and has been "in force every year since 1842" according to the Association of Taxation Technicians; beer and tobacco levies and the precursor to inheritance tax also existed over 100 years ago in the UK. The UK did not have "no national debt" a century ago: in February 1926 Chancellor Winston Churchill told Parliament the national debt was £7,738 million at the end of 1925, and the Office for Budget Responsibility says debt reached 143% of GDP in 1918/19 and "remained high during the interwar years". Full Fact rated the claim partly false.

claim: Airlines in Spain and Russia are warning vaccinated people not to fly because of a high risk of fatal blood clots during high-altitude flights, and vaccinated people can be excluded from air travel.
label: False
ruling: False. There is no evidence any airline is doing this. The article found no evidence of any airline saying this; the claim traces to a 2021 article from a Russian online news portal that offered no evidence of a ban or plans for one, and the International Air Transport Association told Reuters it was not aware of any airlines considering this. No evidence exists that any Covid vaccine raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis while flying.

claim: Henry Kissinger addressed the World Health Organization's "Council on Eugenics" on 25 February 2009, stating that vaccine-makers stand to make millions because "the herd pays us for providing extermination services."
label: False
ruling: False. There is no evidence Henry Kissinger, who died in 2023, ever made this speech. The WHO told Politifact and Africa Check it had no record of such a speech and that the "Council on Eugenics" does not exist. The social media posts provide no other source for the quote, and Kissinger's representatives told Reuters and AFP the claim was a "complete fabrication." Full Fact rated the claim false.

claim: Ethylene oxide, the chemical used to sterilise the swabs used in cervical smear tests, is cancer-causing, so it is dangerous to have a smear test.
label: Misleading
ruling: "For the purposes of that scheme, we've rated this claim as missing context because the implied claim, that smear tests are unsafe due to ethylene oxide, is false." The article also states that "there is no credible evidence it endangers patients who come into contact with sterilised medical devices," and that a Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency spokesperson said "there is no credible evidence that the swabs used in cervical smear tests are associated with cancer."

claim: A Facebook video posted on 17 October shows a woman in Toby Carvery-branded clothing saying that Toby Carvery is giving everyone who likes the post and comments "Yorkie" a free carvery for two to celebrate National Yorkshire Pudding Week.
label: False
ruling: False. The video is not genuine. A spokesperson for Toby Carvery's parent company, Mitchells & Butlers, told Full Fact that this is not a genuine offer from them. Google's SynthID detector also found its watermark in both the video and audio, indicating they were made with Google's AI tools. Full Fact rated the claim false for its Facebook fact-checking scheme.

claim: Facebook posts offering a Waterstones "Bestsellers Box" for £3 after filling out a short questionnaire, or for a small shipping fee after leaving a review, are genuine Waterstones offers.
label: False
ruling: Facebook posts offering cheap "Waterstones Bestsellers Boxes" are not genuine. Both posts link to a site outside the Waterstones website, and the company told Full Fact it does not direct customers to sites other than waterstones.com. Full Fact rated the claim false because Waterstones says it does not direct customers anywhere other than its own website.

claim: A social media post that begins "I am a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee" and describes Donald Trump's efforts to win the Nobel Peace Prize was written by a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, the body that awards the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.
label: False
ruling: This is a satirical post. It was first shared on X by an account that describes themselves as a "satirist" and regularly creates similar content from fictional insiders. A satirical post about US President Donald Trump's efforts to be awarded the Nobel Peace Prize has been shared on Facebook as if it's from an actual Nobel Committee member. The lengthy post begins "I am a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee"... While the post doesn't mention President Trump by name, its description of an award hopeful matches him. It was originally shared on 12 October on X by an account under the name "Peter Girnus", who describes themself in their bio as a "Reader. Writer. Satirist. Hacker." The account regularly shares long posts from fictional insiders, such as employees working for AI companies or government departments.

claim: A video shows people selling items looted during the nationwide unrest in France in October 2026.
label: False
ruling: False. The video was filmed on Gran Vía in Madrid, Spain, and has been online since at least 29 September, before the recent looting seen in France. The video shows street vendors selling designer bags and football shirts, and was shared with false claims that it shows people selling items looted during the unrest in France. Full Fact rated the claim as false because the video was filmed in Madrid and predates the recent unrest in France.

claim: Mainstream medicine ignores natural remedies and naturally occurring therapeutic compounds, and does not use natural compounds to develop treatments.
label: False
ruling: Wellness influencers claim mainstream medicine ignores natural remedies. They're wrong. The article says drug research and development often draws on compounds found in nature, citing penicillin (derived from a Penicillium mold), paclitaxel (from the Pacific yew tree), aspirin (based on salicylic acid from plants such as willow bark), artemisinin (from the herb Artemisia annua), ivermectin (based on avermectin from soil), and cannabidiol (derived from cannabis). It concludes that mainstream medicine "doesn't hesitate to use natural compounds when it comes to seeking new therapies," and that what matters is whether a compound is safe and effective, not where it comes from.

claim: The three taxpayer-funded White House advertisements featuring President Donald Trump, released on or after September 23, 2025, are comparable to federally funded public service announcements that past administrations of both parties, including those of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden, have used to explain policy and make the case for the nation's direction.
label: Misleading
ruling: The White House defended the three ads by pointing to federally funded public service announcements from the Bush, Obama and Biden administrations. The article finds the comparison weak. Legal expert Richard Painter said, "I just think you're not going to find any comparison at all," and called the Trump ads "so clearly propaganda." Political scientist John G. Geer said the ads are "different enough so that I personally don't buy the argument" that they are all the same, and that the Trump ads are more political. The article notes that one cited Obama example, an EPA social media outreach campaign on clean water, was found by the GAO in December 2015 to have violated federal laws on publicity or propaganda and grassroots lobbying. The other cited Obama example, promoting ACA open enrollment, is similar to the Trump ads. The article therefore presents the White House comparison as misleading, since the cited examples differ in purpose and at least one was found unlawful.

claim: Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Maine in 2026, wants to raise Social Security taxes, which would hurt seniors.
label: Misleading
ruling: The language used in the ads could give viewers the false impression that Jackson wants to increase the Social Security payroll tax, or that he wants to raise taxes on Social Security benefits. Neither is Jackson's plan. What Jackson has proposed is changing the amount of annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax by eliminating the cap on taxable earnings ($184,500 for 2026). Current beneficiaries are unlikely to be affected, according to an Urban Institute economist, so the claim that the change would hurt seniors is not supported. The ads' claim is misleading.

claim: Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) voted to give himself a $500,000 taxpayer-funded payout in the November 2025 vote on the bill that ended the government shutdown.
label: Misleading
ruling: "But that's not the whole story, and the ad leaves the false impression that Sullivan received that money." The bill included a provision allowing eight Republican senators, including Sullivan, to seek damages from the federal government over phone toll records obtained during the special counsel's Jan. 6 investigation. Sullivan said he only learned of the provision when reading the bill just before his vote, vowed not to sue, and supported the House repealing the provision, which ultimately happened. The ad's "cashing in" implication is misleading.

claim: In a 2026 campaign ad for Republican U.S. Senator Dan Sullivan in Alaska, Sandy Snodgrass says that Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola "took [contributions] from liberals who opened our borders to the drug cartels" and then "voted with them against securing our border."
label: Misleading
ruling: The ad "leaves out several important points of context." Its claim that lower-48 liberals opened the borders to drug cartels ignores that experts, including government officials, say the vast majority of fentanyl entering the U.S. is smuggled through legal ports of entry, mostly by American citizens. On Peltola, she did vote against the 2023 Republican Secure the Border Act, but the following year she was among a handful of Democrats who joined Republicans in backing a nearly identical bill (the End the Border Catastrophe Act, April 20, 2024), and she often broke with her party on immigration votes. Opposing that bill was not a vote for "open borders," so the ad's portrayal is misleading.

claim: In an advertisement released by Vivek Ramaswamy's Ohio gubernatorial campaign in October 2026, Donna Arthur, the estranged mother of Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton, says that Acton is a liar who lies about her past, and that Acton's claim that she grew up living in a tent is not true.
label: Mostly false
ruling: The article finds that court documents, contemporaneous news reports, and statements by Acton's brother, Philip Stearns, corroborate key elements of Acton's account of her difficult childhood, including her removal from her mother's custody at age 12 after her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her in July 1978. On the tent claim specifically, the article reports that a 1982 police report documents an interview with an Ohio campground manager who said Cledith Arthur had lived at the campground some years earlier, and that 1978 arrest paperwork lists that campground as Arthur's address. The article notes that the Ramaswamy campaign did not respond to questions about the ad. Taken together, the evidence reported contradicts the ad's assertion that none of Acton's account of living in a tent is true and that she has lied throughout her life.

claim: Data centers across the United States are driving up electricity prices.
label: Misleading
ruling: "It's not a given that prices will rise if a data center moves in, but the risk is real — and price increases have already occurred in some places." The article also states: "If many Americans think that all of or even the bulk of their recent electricity price increases are due to data centers, that is a misconception." It adds that at least for the PJM Interconnection, "prices have likely gone up as a result of data centers," while in Texas "it is not entirely clear" and national retail prices rose 29% from 2019 to 2025 (3% after inflation), with fuel prices and grid costs cited as the main drivers.

claim: Wisconsin Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden was "the deciding vote to gut Medicare" through his vote in 2025 for President Donald Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading. The article says Democratic attack ads "misleadingly frame the OBBBA or Republican policies as a major assault on Medicare." It explains that the law's Medicare changes "are narrow in scope and affect relatively few beneficiaries." Those changes include ending Medicare eligibility for some lawfully present immigrants (CBO: 100,000 fewer insured, $5.1 billion less Medicare spending over 10 years) and suspending a Biden-era Medicare Savings Program rule (CBO: 800,000 fewer beneficiaries receiving extra subsidies, $66 billion saved over 10 years, mostly to Medicaid). The article notes the bulk of the OBBBA's large health cuts fell on Medicaid, and that the law's Medicare changes "will not affect benefits or eligibility for the vast majority of enrollees." The article also says the law could have triggered much larger Medicare cuts under PAYGO rules, but Congress routinely waives those rules.

claim: In a September 24, 2026 attack ad, Democratic super PAC WinSenate claimed that Jeffrey Epstein's business partner funneled $3 million to Sen. Susan Collins's super PAC, Pine Tree Results PAC, in the 2026 Maine Senate race.
label: Misleading
ruling: "But to call them 'business partners' is a stretch." The article notes that Stephen Schwarzman gave $3 million total to Pine Tree Results PAC in June 2025 and June 2026, and that he and Epstein were both among the founding members of the Core Club in New York City, which the article says is not the same as having been business partners. "But other than paying money to join and get the club started, it's not clear that Schwarzman and Epstein ever did business together as 'partners,' which implies a close working relationship." A spokesperson for Schwarzman said the men had no relationship. The ad's claim is therefore misleading.

claim: In October 2026, voting machines in multiple U.S. states, including Texas, South Carolina and Tennessee, changed voters' intended Democratic votes to Republican votes.
label: False
ruling: There is no evidence that touchscreen voting machines are deliberately switching voter selections. Rather, elections experts and state election officials have said that reported issues of machines initially not recording votes correctly are a result of familiar machine calibration issues or voter error. Also, nearly the entire country votes in a manner where voters review a paper ballot before having their votes officially cast.

claim: In the 2026 Texas Senate race, Republican Ken Paxton's campaign ad claimed that Democratic opponent James Talarico "backs higher taxes on working families, $3,000 a year. Taxes on your tips, your overtime, even Social Security."
label: Mostly false
ruling: The ad assumes Talarico opposes all of the tax cuts in the OBBBA. He does not. Talarico has said it's time to repeal the big ugly bill's tax breaks for the top 1% and give that money to the middle class, and his campaign says he specifically supports the OBBBA provisions cutting taxes on tips, overtime pay and Social Security. The "$3,000 a year" figure refers to a Tax Foundation estimate of the average tax cut from the OBBBA, which the ad presents as a tax increase. The ad's claim is misleading and not supported by the record; the campaign's own characterization of Talarico as opposing the bill's tax cuts is contradicted by his stated support for the middle-class provisions.

claim: In a Senate Leadership Fund ad airing in the 2026 New Hampshire Senate race beginning October 24, 2026, the narrator says that Democratic U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas's net worth is "up by upwards of 1,000%" while he has served in Congress, with on-screen figures showing it went from as low as negative $669,974 in 2018 to over $6 million in 2025.
label: False
ruling: The ad falsely claims Pappas' net worth shot up by 1,000% while in office, a figure that could only be replicated with misleading math. Financial disclosure forms show the increase in his net worth was much more modest, and mostly due to listing his husband's assets on more recent disclosure forms. The 2018 figure comes from subtracting the high-end estimate of liabilities from the low-end estimate of assets, and the 2025 figure reverses that, cherry-picking the ranges; flipping the same method could show his net worth fell by millions.

claim: James Talarico, while a member of the Texas House of Representatives, voted for an income tax in Texas.
label: False
ruling: Talarico didn't vote for an income tax. Rather, he opposed a 2019 joint resolution in the Texas Legislature calling for a constitutional amendment to prohibit an individual income tax. Texas doesn't have such a tax. The article notes the 2019 amendment, which voters approved, made implementing an income tax harder, and that Talarico said the state income tax was "already banned" and that he is "against an income tax in Texas, always have been."

claim: In a 2026 ad paid for by the National Republican Senatorial Committee, a woman says Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed "supported defunding our police" and then "called for abolishing prisons and releasing criminals into our neighborhoods."
label: Misleading
ruling: The ads either omit context or exaggerate his past policy proposals. El-Sayed did embrace elements of the "defund the police" movement in 2020, but while campaigning for the 2026 Senate seat he has talked about investing in, not defunding, law enforcement. He has not "called for abolishing prisons," and "never said he favored 'abolishing prisons.'" The ad's clip comes from an August 2020 webinar in which he discussed reducing the prison population during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and his fuller remarks do not support the claim.

claim: In 2026, Texas PAC, an advertising group associated with the Senate Leadership Fund, said that James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas and a Texas state representative, "supported using taxpayer dollars for sex change surgeries on young children."
label: Misleading
ruling: The article says that in several congressional races, Republican ads claiming Democratic candidates support "sex changes" for children or taxpayer funding of such surgeries are flawed. For Texas, it says the Texas PAC ads cite Talarico's vote against a 2023 state law that broadly prohibited gender-affirming medications and surgeries for minors and barred state money for them, while Talarico voted for an amendment that would have limited the bill to banning surgeries. The article notes Talarico's campaign said he opposes gender reassignment surgery for minors, and that Talarico told Fox News he opposed the 2023 bill as "overly broad" and voted for a major amendment to limit it to surgeries. The article also says the ads leave out that the surgeries at issue are typically performed after age 18.

claim: Crystal Mason was sentenced to five years in prison for illegal voting because of Ken Paxton's crackdown on voters of color.
label: Misleading
ruling: The ad's claim is misleading. Mason was convicted and sentenced in March 2018 for casting a provisional ballot in the 2016 general election while ineligible, and she was on supervised release for a 2011 tax fraud felony. Her case was investigated and prosecuted by the Tarrant County District Attorney's Office, not Paxton's office, and the judge gave no explanation for the five-year sentence. Paxton's office did conduct a broader voter fraud crackdown that disproportionately targeted people of color according to an ACLU analysis, but that analysis did not include Mason's case, so the ad's link between her sentence and Paxton's crackdown lacks support and context.

claim: In early October 2026, James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, was a patient at the Lindner Center of Hope, a mental health center in Mason, Ohio.
label: False
ruling: No. An Ohio mental health center rebutted false online rumors that Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, had been there as a patient. Talarico said he was off the campaign trail for several days in early October while recovering from the flu at his Texas home.

claim: At an Oct. 5, 2026 rally in Nebraska, President Donald Trump, saying "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego," was advocating an attack on Los Angeles and San Diego and presenting the destruction of those two cities as an acceptable cost.
label: Mostly false
ruling: Not our reading of the president's comments. While his wording is confusing, a more plausible interpretation is that he meant the war would prevent Iran from posing a threat to U.S. cities, and higher gas prices are a small sacrifice to make. Taken in context, his remarks don't appear to be "advocating" an attack on U.S. cities or suggesting their destruction would be an acceptable cost. He has made versions of those points before, using similar language.

claim: The Biden administration's 2024 power plant rule, which limited greenhouse gas emissions from existing coal-fired power plants and new natural gas plants, threatened the reliability of the U.S. electrical grid and purposefully targeted reliable baseload power for extinction, as stated by EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin at a September 14 (2025) event in Houston announcing the rule's revocation.
label: Misleading
ruling: Trump administration officials have misleadingly cast the prior administration's policy as a threat to grid reliability. Experts say that's unfounded. Nor do experts think that the power plant regulations posed a threat to the reliability of the electrical grid. The 2024 power plant rule might have led some coal plants to retire earlier than they would have otherwise, but coal plants were already facing unfavorable economic headwinds, and rescinding the regulations is "not going to tip the general trajectory of coal plants."

claim: The Trump administration's "most favored nation" prescription drug pricing deals with pharmaceutical companies are rescuing state budgets and will save Medicaid over $64 billion over a decade, as estimated by the White House Council of Economic Advisers, as stated by President Donald Trump, Medicare and Medicaid administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. at a September 18, 2026 White House event.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading. The $64 billion figure does come from a May White House Council of Economic Advisers report, which projected savings of about that much over 10 years, split between the federal government and the states. But experts say the estimate's assumptions are unclear and it is unknown which drugs will be covered, how many states will participate, and how long arrangements will last; drugmakers have indicated the agreements cover only some products. Medicaid already receives large discounts, and the White House projects savings to states of under 2% of annual Medicaid spending initially, diminishing over time. The article concludes it is "an exaggeration to suggest this program will single-handedly save state budgets, even under the rosiest of scenarios," and that "a healthy dose of skepticism is warranted."

claim: Kansas Sen. Roger Marshall, the Republican incumbent, voted to keep the Jeffrey Epstein files sealed and thereby helped cover up Epstein's crimes, as claimed in WinSenate ads running in the 2026 Kansas Senate race.
label: Misleading
ruling: Misleading. The article says Democratic-group ads "misleadingly claim" Marshall helped cover up Epstein's crimes by voting to keep the files under wraps. Marshall supported the November 2025 law requiring the Justice Department to release the files, and he voted against a September 2025 Senate Democratic amendment to the defense policy bill that would have directed their release. He said he opposed tying the release to an unrelated defense bill, calling it a "political stunt," and two months later he supported a standalone release bill that passed the Senate by unanimous consent. The ads "don't give a full account" of his votes on the issue.

claim: In U.S. elections ahead of the 2026 midterms, any ballot that a poll worker marks at the polling place, with a letter, checkmark, star, "R," "D," or any other writing, will be disqualified.
label: False
ruling: The rumor is not true. Many election officials have clarified that a poll worker marking a ballot does not disqualify it. It was not possible to find any evidence of a U.S. state disqualifying ballots containing markings, unless it renders the voter's selections unreadable. Several states (such as North Carolina) actually require poll workers to mark ballots as part of the verification process.

claim: In the days before the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, Darline Graham, the South Carolina senator who filled the Senate vacancy left by her brother Lindsey Graham's death in July 2026, said she did not want to be a senator and that, "When I get to heaven one day, I am just going to choke Lindsey."
label: Contested
ruling: The claim was a mixture of true and false elements. It was true that Graham said during a radio interview (at 34:00) on Oct. 28 that, "When I get to heaven one day, I am just going to choke Lindsey." However, there was no evidence that Graham ever said she did not want to be a senator. She had reportedly said at a campaign event the day before that "I actually love the job," speaking about her time in the Senate. Rather, Graham appeared to be expressing frustration at the timing of her appointment and intense primary election campaign due to her brother's unexpected death when she said she wanted to choke him.

claim: President Donald Trump said at a political rally in Ohio, shortly before the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, that Democrats "want to make Ohio a state."
label: True
ruling: The video is real — Trump really did say Democrats want to "make Ohio a state." The remark was made at a rally in Swanton, Ohio, near Toledo, which also featured Vice President JD Vance, and it is captured in C-SPAN's coverage. Trump likely meant to refer to the U.S. territory of Puerto Rico, which has long debated its political status, but he did say Ohio.

claim: In late October 2026, the U.S. Army trained soldiers to dig mass battlefield graves for American troops as the U.S. war on Iran continued, with the training meant to prepare for mass casualties.
label: Misleading
ruling: Both the image and the claim were real. The images were distributed by the Department of Defense's media distribution service on Oct. 22, 2026, and show a simulated temporary interment trench exercise (Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant, Oct. 21, 2026) near the St. Mere Eglise Drop Zone. However, it wasn't clear precisely what the exercise was in preparation for, and the conclusions some people drew about an imminent or specific threat originated from social media, not the Army itself.

claim: In 2017, actor Patrick Stewart said of U.S. President Donald Trump: "The fact is, when America sneezes, the world catches a cold. America, I think, is on the edge of a very bad flu infection, and it's because of the man who is in the White House."
label: True
ruling: The quote is correctly attributed to Stewart. It originates from a video interview he gave to The A.V. Club, an online entertainment website, which published on Nov. 16, 2017, roughly 10 months into Trump's first presidential term. The A.V. Club posted several other clips from the same interview around that time, and the outlet published them before generative AI was widely available, so there is no reason to suspect the footage is AI-generated.

claim: Vivek Ramaswamy was booed off the stage during his keynote speech at the Young Americans for Liberty convention in Cleveland, Ohio, on July 29, 2026, after saying that people in his generation who had already made it were going to be fine.
label: Misleading
ruling: The claim is a mixture of true, false and undetermined elements. The speech was authentic, but occurred on July 29, during a conference for the libertarian youth group Young Americans for Liberty. Some posts slightly misquoted Ramaswamy, making it appear he said all members of his generation had "made it" and were going to be "fine"; the video shows he said "people in my generation who have already made it, we're going to be fine." Social media clips implied he left the stage because of the cold reception to that line, but the full video shows he was booed throughout his appearance, and after the phrase (12:20 into the speech) he continued speaking for another minute and 16 seconds before putting down the microphone and leaving the stage, followed by more boos. Whether he cut his speech short cannot be determined without the intended full remarks.

claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that authorities would "look into Abdul El-Sayed's immigration status and see if he committed fraud," in the days before the November 3, 2026 U.S. midterm elections, while El-Sayed, a Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate from Michigan, was running in that race.
label: False
ruling: "We found no evidence in searches on Google, Yahoo and DuckDuckGo ... that Rubio said he or the State Department was investigating El-Sayed's immigration status. Given El-Sayed's prominent position as a rare Muslim candidate in a race in a crucial swing state, reputable media outlets would have reported on such an investigation. Therefore, we found social media users incorrectly attributed the quote to Rubio." The claim appeared to come from a Facebook page that described some of its content as satirical, and El-Sayed was born in Rochester Hills, Michigan, on Oct. 31, 1984, so he never had an immigration status for Rubio or the State Department to investigate.

claim: A video recorded during the 2026 U.S. midterm elections shows a touch screen voting machine changing a vote for Democratic candidate Tobi Beck to the Republican challenger, Jim Baird.
label: Misleading
ruling: Miscaptioned. The video appeared genuine and showed no signs of AI or digital manipulation, but it was reportedly recorded during the 2018 midterms, not 2026, at a polling place in Tippecanoe County, Indiana. Democratic and Republican officials attributed such matters to improper touch screen calibration and reported no widespread or deliberate voting issues. Tippecanoe County's elections specialist called the claims of vote switching "patently false" and the old video "deceptive" and "misleading."

claim: U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., married her brother, a man named Ahmed Elmi, in order to commit immigration fraud.
label: Unproven
ruling: The claim that Omar married her brother is unfounded. Snopes found the claims lack evidence because they appear to be entirely circumstantial and unsubstantiated. Similar names do not prove Omar is related to Leila Nur Said or Ahmed Elmi, the claims did not confirm Ahmed Elmi's parentage or his relationship to Leila Nur Said, and they ignore Somali naming conventions. Snopes concluded that this was not evidence enough to support the claim she married her brother or committed immigration fraud. Snopes said it would update the report if more information surfaced.

claim: In 2026, staffers for Alaska Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Mary Peltola spent months recruiting candidates named Dan Sullivan to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, in order to draw votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, as reported by The New York Times on Oct. 28, 2026.
label: Unproven
ruling: We have no reason to doubt the veracity of the Times' reporting. However, because we were unable to view the evidence or obtain additional confirmation from people involved, we cannot confirm its claims as of this writing.

claim: Emergency preparedness guidelines released by multiple governments in and around October 2026, including the United Kingdom, the United States, and Japan, signal that a catastrophic event is about to occur.
label: False
ruling: The claim that emergency preparation guidelines that multiple countries released in and around October 2026 signal a catastrophic event is about to occur is unfounded. It's true that countries including the United Kingdom, the United States and Japan released new or updated emergency preparedness campaigns or programs in 2026. However, such announcements are nothing new. The European Union released a new emergency preparedness strategy in 2025, and many European countries were simply falling in line with the new EU guidance by releasing new messaging. The claim is based in some truth, but the implication that these recommendations mean a catastrophic or destabilizing global event is looming is unfounded.

claim: U.S. President Donald Trump sexually abused Dr. Larissa Portnoff, a New York state licensed psychologist, when she was a minor, beginning when she was around 8 years old, as she alleged in an Instagram video posted on October 30, 2026.
label: Unproven
ruling: Snopes is unable to rate the allegations as true or false. The article states: "It was not possible to independently verify Portnoff's abuse and intimidation allegations against Trump and others in what she described as 'his inner circle.'" It adds that the allegations "have not been tried in a court of law, as of this writing," that the anonymous complaint is not public record so it could not be verified whether any authority is investigating, and that "Based on the currently available evidence, Snopes is unable to rate the allegations as true or false." White House spokesperson Lauren Bis called the claims "false and slanderous" and said "President Trump has never even met or heard of this woman."

claim: In February 1926, Chancellor of the Exchequer Winston Churchill told Parliament that the UK's national debt was £7,738 million at the end of 1925.
label: True
ruling: corrected statement

claim: The International Air Transport Association (IATA) told Reuters that it was not aware of any airlines considering barring vaccinated people from flying.
label: True
ruling: corrected statement

claim: Henry Kissinger's representatives told Reuters and AFP that a quotation circulating under his name was a "complete fabrication."
label: True
ruling: corrected statement

claim: Mitchells & Butlers, the parent company of Toby Carvery, has said that it did not make the free-carvery-for-two offer advertised in a Facebook video posted on 17 October, and Google's SynthID detector found its watermark in both the video and audio, indicating they were made with Google's AI tools.
label: True
ruling: corrected statement

claim: Waterstones told Full Fact that it does not direct customers to any website other than waterstones.com.
label: True
ruling: corrected statement

claim: A satirical post beginning "I am a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee," which describes Donald Trump's efforts to win the Nobel Peace Prize, was first shared on X on 12 October by an account under the name "Peter Girnus," which describes itself in its bio as "Reader. Writer. Satirist. Hacker."
label: True
ruling: corrected statement

claim: A video filmed on Gran Vía in Madrid, Spain, shows street vendors selling designer bags and football shirts, and it has been online since at least 29 September 2026.
